nameStory: The Curved-toothed Geometer gets its name from the distinctive jagged, curved edges on its forewings that look like tiny teeth. The "geometer" part comes from the way its caterpillars move - they arch their backs and "measure" the earth with their bodies as they crawl, like little living rulers. The scientific name Eutrapela clemataria references clematis vines, one of their host plants.
description: The Curved-toothed Geometer Moth is a medium-sized brown moth with distinctively scalloped wing edges that give it its common name. With a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2.2 inches, it displays muted purplish-brown coloration that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. This moth is actually the only species in its genus Eutrapela, making it quite unique among New England's geometer moths. Like all geometers, its caterpillars are "inchworms" that loop along branches in their characteristic measuring motion.

idTips.label: Scalloped wing edges
idTips.description: The forewings have distinctly curved, tooth-like projections along the outer edges that feel slightly rough to the touch, unlike most moths with smooth wing margins

idTips.label: Purplish-brown coloration
idTips.description: Wings display a muted brownish color with subtle purplish undertones that shift slightly in different lighting, feeling velvety when gently touched

idTips.label: Medium wingspan
idTips.description: Wings span about 1.5-2.2 inches across when fully open, roughly the size of a silver dollar, with forewings noticeably longer than hindwings

idTips.label: Bark-like patterns
idTips.description: Wing surfaces show subtle mottled patterns resembling tree bark texture, with fine lines and darker patches that help camouflage against rough bark

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings horizontally against tree trunks with body pressed flat, creating a triangular silhouette

habitat: Look for Curved-toothed Geometers in deciduous and mixed woodlands throughout New England, especially areas with oak, maple, and birch trees. They're commonly found in both mature forests and younger second-growth woods, from sea level to mid-elevations in the mountains. The moths rest on tree bark during the day and are attracted to lights near wooded areas at night.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with peak flight activity starting in May. Look for them resting on tree bark during warm days or flying to lights on mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak adult activity occurs through summer months when they're most commonly seen at porch lights and moth sheets. Caterpillars are actively feeding on deciduous tree leaves during this time.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight continues into early fall, with some individuals still active in September. Late-season caterpillars are preparing to pupate for winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active during winter months. The species overwinters as pupae in leaf litter and soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: This moth is the sole representative of its entire genus in North America - it's literally one of a kind! While most moth genera contain dozens or even hundreds of species, Eutrapela clemataria stands completely alone in its evolutionary branch, making every individual you spot a living representative of a unique lineage that has no close cousins.
confusionNotes: The scalloped wing edges make this species fairly distinctive among New England geometers, but it might be confused with some of the larger brown geometers like the Large Maple Spanworm Moth. Remember the memory trick: "Curved teeth, curved wings" - those distinctive scalloped edges are the giveaway that separates it from other brown forest moths.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "geometer," this moth family name doesn't refer to mathematical geometry but rather to the measuring motion of their caterpillars. The term comes from Greek words meaning "earth measurer," perfectly describing how the inchworm caterpillars seem to measure distances as they loop along branches.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus, compare it to other medium-sized brown geometer moths in New England. Most other geometers in the family lack the distinctive scalloped wing edges and tend to have smoother wing margins. The Curved-toothed Geometer's unique wing shape and purplish-brown coloration set it apart from its more angular or gray-toned relatives in the broader geometer family.
